newsitem.title: USA: SORGHUM--Huge Kansas crop eases pain of lost wheat.
newsitem.headline: SORGHUM--Huge Kansas crop eases pain of lost wheat.

text.p: After high winds slashed and killed much of the Kansas wheat crop last spring, farmers let the dust settle, plowed up the damaged wheat and planted sorghum.
Now, thanks to timely summer rains, they are reaping huge sorghum yields that should return a record harvest for the state, the nation's largest producer.
"It turned out to be one of the better cash years our producers have had," said Gary Fair, executive director of the Sumner County Farm Service Agency.
Not only are farmers reporting bountiful yields, but the quality of the grain is the highest in many years.
"The test weights are the best I have ever seen," said a Salina, Kan., grain dealer.

Yields of 100 bushels per acre or more are common this year as are test weights from 56 to 60 lbs per bushel, grain dealers said. The Kansas harvest is about 80 percent complete and many central Kansas grain elevators are flooded with grain and have had to pile thousands of bushels on the ground.
Kansas farmers planted 4.8 million acres of sorghum last spring, up 45 percent from 3.3 million the previous year.
The increase was largely because farmers replaced damaged wheat with sorghum.

The Kansas Agricultural Statistics Service estimated that acreage will produce 349.6 million bushels, which would exceed the 1986 record of 311.25 million. Statewide yields should average 76 bushels per acre versus 56 bushels a year ago.
The No. 2 producer, Texas, should have a large crop as well, estimated by the state at 191.1 million bushels versus 129.6 million a year ago.
The high quality of this year's crop, plus the competitive prices, has cattlemen from Kansas to Texas increasing the percentage of sorghum in feed rations.
"I would think you would see some shifting to milo (sorghum) this year in feedyard rations," said Sid Love, grain analyst with Kropf-Love Consulting.
Love said sorghum provides 90 percent of the nutrients that corn does, but that percentage may be higher this year because of high quality of the crop.

In Kansas, sorghum is selling for about $2.00 per bushel versus $2.40 for corn, which makes sorghum a price-competive feed alternative, said Kansas grain dealers. Some of the Kansas sorghum is even being shipped to Texas feedlots, said Texas cattle sources.

Love said the bountiful Kansas harvest should prompt the U.S. Agriculture Department to increase its U.S. sorghum crop estimate to about 830 million bushels in next week's crop production report, to be released November 12. In October, USDA estimated the sorghum crop at 797 million bushels.
